knitr::include_graphics("cover.png")

## 1. Introduction

The concept of ESG investing — incorporating Environmental, Social, and 
Governance criteria into investment decisions — has grown substantially 
over the past decade. Between 2020 and 2021, ESG-labelled funds attracted 
record inflows as institutional and retail investors increasingly 
prioritised sustainability alongside financial returns. However, the period 
that followed presented a markedly different environment. Rising interest 
rates from 2022 onwards disproportionately affected growth-oriented and 
ESG-heavy sectors such as technology and renewable energy, while a growing 
wave of institutional scepticism toward ESG products contributed to 
significant outflows from ESG funds.

This shifting landscape raises an important empirical question: did ESG 
indices actually behave differently from their conventional counterparts 
during this period, and if so, can any differences be explained by the 
interest rate environment?

This paper investigates the return and volatility dynamics of ESG-screened 
equity indices relative to conventional benchmarks across two market 
pairs — one US and one global — over the period January 2020 to December 
2024. We apply a structured time series framework including descriptive 
analysis, stationarity testing, autocorrelation analysis, GARCH volatility 
modelling, and regime analysis across pre- and post-2022 subsamples.

---

## 2. Literature Review

Research on the financial performance of ESG investments relative to 
conventional benchmarks has grown substantially alongside the rise of 
sustainable investing. Friede, Busch and Bassen (2015) conducted a 
meta-analysis of over 2,000 empirical studies and found that the large 
majority reported a non-negative relationship between ESG criteria and 
corporate financial performance, suggesting that ESG investing does not 
systematically destroy value.

More recent work has focused on the dynamic relationship between ESG 
and conventional indices during periods of market stress. Ashraf (2020)
demonstrated that stock markets responded negatively to 
rising COVID-19 case numbers across 64 countries, with the strongest 
negative reaction occurring in the early stages of the outbreak.

Albuquerque et al.(2020) further showed that stocks with higher environmental
and social ratings exhibited significantly higher returns and lower volatility 
during the COVID-19 market crash of Q1 2020, suggesting that ESG 
screening may confer resilience during periods of acute market stress.

Albuquerque et al. (2020) attribute this resilience to stronger customer 
and investor loyalty among ESG firms, which dampens both revenue 
volatility and selling pressure during market stress.

However, the relationship between ESG performance and the interest rate 
environment has received comparatively less attention. Pastor, Stambaugh 
and Taylor (2022) show that green stocks are structurally aligned with 
growth and negatively correlated with value stocks, and that lower 
expected returns for green assets are consistent with theory. This 
structural tilt suggests that rising interest rates — which historically 
favour value over growth — may systematically disadvantage ESG indices 
relative to conventional benchmarks, a hypothesis we test empirically 
in this paper.

---

## 3. Research Question and Hypotheses

Our central research question is:

> **Did the return and volatility dynamics of ESG indices change relative 
> to conventional indices during the 2022–2024 rising interest rate period?**

We explore this through the following hypotheses:

**H1:** ESG indices exhibit different return behaviour compared to 
conventional indices during the 2022–2024 period.
univariate descriptive

**H2:** ESG indices exhibit different volatility dynamics compared to 
conventional indices.
univariate dynamic

**H3:** The relationship between ESG and conventional indices differs 
between the pre-2022 and post-2022 subsamples.
multivariate
---
## 4. Data and Methodology

# 4.1 Data Setup

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

library(quantmod)
library(zoo)
library(xts)
library(ggplot2)
library(moments)
library(reshape2)
library(kableExtra)
library(vars)
```

```{r parameters}
start_date <- "2020-01-01"
end_date   <- "2024-12-31"
```

We created the date parameters for data retrieval from the Yahoo website, which can interact with R through "quantmod" package.

```{r pull-equity-data}
getSymbols("ESGU",    from = start_date, to = end_date, src = "yahoo")
getSymbols("^GSPC",   from = start_date, to = end_date, src = "yahoo")
getSymbols("IWDA.AS", from = start_date, to = end_date, src = "yahoo")
getSymbols("SUWS.L",  from = start_date, to = end_date, src = "yahoo")
```

```{r pull-rate-data}
getSymbols("DGS10", src = "FRED", from = start_date, to = end_date)
```

```{r extract-prices}
esgu <- Ad(ESGU)
gspc <- Ad(GSPC)
iwda <- Ad(IWDA.AS)
suws <- Ad(SUWS.L)
rate <- DGS10
```

```{r check-data, include=FALSE}
head(esgu)
head(gspc)
head(iwda)
head(suws)
head(rate)
```

### 4.2 Data Sources and Collection

The dataset comprises five daily time series covering the period from 
2 January 2020 to 31 December 2024, yielding 1,304 trading day 
observations after cleaning. Two pairs of ESG and conventional indices 
are used: the iShares ESG Aware MSCI USA ETF (ESGU) versus the S&P 500 
(^GSPC) for the US market, and the iShares MSCI World ESG Leaders ETF 
(SUWS.L) versus the iShares Core MSCI World ETF (IWDA.AS) for the global 
market. The 10-year US Treasury yield (DGS10) is included as a proxy for 
the interest rate environment. All equity data is sourced via the Yahoo 
Finance API using the quantmod package in R. Interest rate data is 
sourced from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) platform.

The series are denominated in different currencies and price scales. 
This is expected and does not affect the analysis, as all subsequent 
calculations are based on log returns rather than price levels.

### 4.2 Data Cleaning and Preparation

```{r merge-and-rename}
all_data <- merge(esgu, gspc, iwda, suws, rate)
colnames(all_data) <- c("ESGU", "GSPC", "IWDA", "SUWS", "Rate_10Y")
```

After merging, missing values were identified across all series due to 
differences in trading calendars between US and European markets. US 
markets observe different public holidays to Dutch and UK markets, 
resulting in non-overlapping non-trading days. Missing values were 
handled by carrying the last available observation forward using 
na.locf(), which is standard practice in financial time series analysis.

```{r check-nas, include=FALSE}
colSums(is.na(all_data))
```

```{r clean-data}
all_data <- na.locf(all_data)
all_data <- na.omit(all_data)
```

```{r check-quality, include=FALSE}
colSums(all_data <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
index(all_data)[1]
index(all_data)[nrow(all_data)]
nrow(all_data)
```

Following cleaning, the dataset runs from 2 January 2020 to 31 December 
2024, comprising 1,304 trading days — consistent with approximately 260 
trading days per year over five years. No zero or negative prices were 
identified, confirming data integrity.

Log returns are computed for all equity series using the formula:

$$r_t = \ln(Y_t) - \ln(Y_{t-1})$$
Log returns are preferred over simple percentage returns as they are 
additive over time and more closely approximate a normal distribution, 
making them better suited for time series modelling. For the interest 
rate series, the first difference of the yield level is used rather 
than log returns, as the rate is already expressed as a percentage.

```{r compute-returns}
log_returns <- diff(log(all_data))
log_returns <- na.omit(log_returns)
rate_diff   <- diff(all_data$Rate_10Y)
rate_diff   <- na.omit(rate_diff)
```

```{r save-data}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(as.data.frame(all_data),    "data/prices.csv",      row.names = TRUE)
write.csv(as.data.frame(log_returns), "data/log_returns.csv", row.names = TRUE)
write.csv(as.data.frame(rate_diff),   "data/rate_diff.csv",   row.names = TRUE)
```

### 4.3 Analytical Methods

The analysis follows a structured time series pipeline. First, 
descriptive analysis is conducted to compare return distributions, 
rolling volatility, and drawdowns across ESG and conventional series. 
Second, Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests are applied to confirm 
stationarity of the transformed series before modelling. Third, 
autocorrelation (ACF) and partial autocorrelation (PACF) functions are 
examined to assess dependence structures. Fourth, GARCH(1,1) models are 
estimated to capture volatility clustering and persistence within each 
series. Fifth, a regime analysis compares pre-2022 and post-2022 
subsamples to evaluate whether return and volatility dynamics changed 
with the interest rate environment. Finally, a VAR model is used to 
examine dynamic interactions between the ESG-conventional performance 
spread and the interest rate series.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 Descriptive Analysis

#### 5.1.1 Summary Statistics

The table below presents key distributional statistics for the log 
return series of all four equity indices over the full sample period 
from January 2020 to December 2024.

```{r descriptive-stats}
library(moments)

desc_stats <- data.frame(
  Series   = c("ESGU", "GSPC", "IWDA", "SUWS"),
  Mean     = c(0.00050, 0.00046, 0.00046, 0.00038),
  Std_Dev  = c(0.01343, 0.01326, 0.01052, 0.01159),
  Skewness = c(-0.806, -0.832, -0.926, -0.656),
  Kurtosis = c(17.436, 17.780, 13.639, 10.573),
  Min      = c(-0.1279, -0.1277, -0.0935, -0.1007),
  Max      = c(0.0925, 0.0897, 0.0805, 0.0773)
)

knitr::kable(desc_stats,
             col.names = c("Series", "Mean", "Std Dev", 
                           "Skewness", "Kurtosis", "Min", "Max"),
             caption = "Table 1: Descriptive Statistics of Daily Log Returns (Jan 2020 – Dec 2024)",
             digits = 5,
             align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
                full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

All four series exhibit negative skewness, indicating that large 
negative returns occur more frequently than large positive returns — 
a common finding in equity return data. The kurtosis values exceed 3 
for all series, indicating fat tails relative to the normal distribution. 
This suggests that extreme return events occur more frequently than a 
normal distribution would predict, which is consistent with the 
turbulent market conditions observed during the sample period including 
the COVID-19 shock in 2020 and the rate hiking cycle beginning in 2022.

#### 5.1.2 Price Level Visualisation

```{r price-plot}
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

# Convert to data frame for ggplot
prices_df <- data.frame(
  Date = index(all_data),
  ESGU = as.numeric(all_data$ESGU),
  GSPC = as.numeric(all_data$GSPC),
  IWDA = as.numeric(all_data$IWDA),
  SUWS = as.numeric(all_data$SUWS)
)

# Normalise to 100 at start so all series are comparable
prices_df[, 2:5] <- sweep(prices_df[, 2:5], 2, 
                           as.numeric(prices_df[1, 2:5]), "/") * 100

prices_long <- melt(prices_df, id.vars = "Date", 
                    variable.name = "Series", value.name = "Price")

ggplot(prices_long, aes(x = Date, y = Price, colour = Series)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2022-01-01"), 
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2022-03-01"), y = 80, 
           label = "Rate hiking begins", size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "Normalised Price Series (Base = 100, January 2020)",
       x = "Date", y = "Indexed Price") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### 5.1.3 Log Returns Visualisation

```{r returns-plot}
returns_df <- data.frame(
  Date = index(log_returns),
  ESGU = as.numeric(log_returns$ESGU),
  GSPC = as.numeric(log_returns$GSPC),
  IWDA = as.numeric(log_returns$IWDA),
  SUWS = as.numeric(log_returns$SUWS)
)

returns_long <- melt(returns_df, id.vars = "Date",
                     variable.name = "Series", value.name = "Return")

ggplot(returns_long, aes(x = Date, y = Return, colour = Series)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2022-01-01"), 
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Daily Log Returns",
       x = "Date", y = "Log Return") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Figure \@ref(fig:returns-plot) plots the daily log returns for all 
four indices over the full sample period. The most prominent feature is the
sharp clustering of large positive and negative returns in early 2020,
coinciding with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Returns during this period
reach magnitudes of  approximately ±10%, far exceeding typical daily variation.
This volatility cluster dissipates over the course of 2020 and returns remain
relatively 
subdued through 2021.

Following the onset of the rate-hiking cycle in early 2022 (dashed vertical 
line), a modest but visible increase in return variability is observed across 
all series, consistent with heightened macroeconomic uncertainty during this 
period. Crucially, the four series track each other closely throughout, with 
no obvious divergence between ESG and conventional indices — suggesting that 
ESG screening does not substantially alter the return dynamics of the 
underlying market exposure.

#### 5.1.4 Rolling Volatility

Rolling volatility measures how the riskiness of each series changes 
over time. We compute a 30-day rolling standard deviation of log returns 
for each series to visualise volatility clustering across the sample period.

```{r rolling-volatility}
library(zoo)

roll_vol <- data.frame(
  Date = index(log_returns),
  ESGU = rollapply(log_returns$ESGU, width = 30, FUN = sd, fill = NA),
  GSPC = rollapply(log_returns$GSPC, width = 30, FUN = sd, fill = NA),
  IWDA = rollapply(log_returns$IWDA, width = 30, FUN = sd, fill = NA),
  SUWS = rollapply(log_returns$SUWS, width = 30, FUN = sd, fill = NA)
)

roll_vol_long <- melt(roll_vol, id.vars = "Date",
                      variable.name = "Series", value.name = "Volatility")

ggplot(roll_vol_long, aes(x = Date, y = Volatility, colour = Series)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2022-01-01"), 
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2022-03-01"), y = 0.025, 
           label = "Rate hiking begins", size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "30-Day Rolling Volatility of Log Returns",
       x = "Date", y = "Rolling Std Dev") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The rolling volatility chart reveals two clear spikes — the first 
corresponding to the COVID-19 market shock in March 2020, and the 
second to the onset of the rate hiking cycle in early 2022. Both 
ESG and conventional series show similar volatility patterns, though 
the relative magnitude of these spikes across pairs will be examined 
more formally in the regime analysis in Section 5.5.

### 5.2 Stationarity Testing

Before applying time series models, the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) 
test is applied to confirm the stationarity properties of each series. 
The null hypothesis of the ADF test is that the series is non-stationary. 
A p-value below 0.05 allows us to reject the null and conclude the series 
is stationary.

#### 5.2.1 ADF Test on Price Levels


```{r stationarity-levels, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tseries)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

run_adf <- function(series, name) {
  result <- adf.test(na.omit(series))
  data.frame(
    Series     = name,
    `ADF Stat` = round(result$statistic, 4),
    `Lag Order` = result$parameter,
    `p-value`  = round(result$p.value, 4),
    Result     = ifelse(result$p.value < 0.05, "Stationary", "Non-stationary"),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

levels_table <- rbind(
  run_adf(all_data$ESGU,     "ESGU"),
  run_adf(all_data$GSPC,     "GSPC"),
  run_adf(all_data$IWDA,     "IWDA"),
  run_adf(all_data$SUWS,     "SUWS"),
  run_adf(all_data$Rate_10Y, "Rate_10Y")
)

kable(levels_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr",
      caption = "ADF Test Results — Price Levels") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(5, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = "H0: series has a unit root (non-stationary). Rejection at p < 0.05 indicates stationarity.",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)
```

As expected, the ADF test results for all price level series return 
p-values above 0.05, confirming that the raw price series are 
non-stationary. This means we cannot use price levels directly in our 
models and must transform the series before proceeding.

#### 5.2.2 ADF Test on Log Returns

```{r stationarity-returns, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tseries)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

returns_table <- rbind(
  run_adf(log_returns$ESGU,  "ESGU"),
  run_adf(log_returns$GSPC,  "GSPC"),
  run_adf(log_returns$IWDA,  "IWDA"),
  run_adf(log_returns$SUWS,  "SUWS"),
  run_adf(rate_diff,         "Rate_10Y (differenced)")
)

kable(returns_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr",
      caption = "ADF Test Results — Log Returns") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(5, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = "H0: series has a unit root (non-stationary). All return series reject H0 at p < 0.05, confirming stationarity.",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)
```

The ADF test results for all log return series return p-values below 
0.05, confirming that the transformed series are stationary and suitable 
for use in subsequent modelling steps. For the interest rate series, the 
first difference of the yield level is used rather than log returns, as 
the rate is already expressed as a percentage.

#### 5.2.3 Summary of Stationarity Results

```{r stationarity-summary}
stationarity_summary <- data.frame(
  Series = c("ESGU (price)", "GSPC (price)", "IWDA (price)", 
             "SUWS (price)", "Rate 10Y (level)",

knitr::kable(stationarity_summary,
             col.names = c("Series", "Dickey-Fuller Statistic", 
                           "p-value", "Stationary"),
             caption = "Table 2: ADF Test Results — Price Levels and Log Returns",
             digits = 3,
             align = c("l", "r", "r", "c"),
             booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"),
                full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE) |>
  row_spec(5, extra_latex_after = "\\midrule")
```

### 5.3 Autocorrelation Analysis

Autocorrelation analysis examines whether past values of a time series 
are correlated with future values. In financial return series, we expect 
little to no autocorrelation in returns themselves — consistent with 
weak-form market efficiency — but significant autocorrelation in squared 
returns, which would indicate volatility clustering and justify the use 
of GARCH modelling.

We examine the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) and Partial Autocorrelation 
Function (PACF) for both the log return series and the squared log return 
series of each index.

```{r acf-returns, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap="ACF of daily log returns — bars outside the blue bands indicate significant autocorrelation."}
library(xts)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$ESGU)), main = "ACF — ESGU", lag.max = 30)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$GSPC)), main = "ACF — GSPC", lag.max = 30)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$IWDA)), main = "ACF — IWDA", lag.max = 30)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$SUWS)), main = "ACF — SUWS", lag.max = 30)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
The ACF plots for the log return series confirm that there is no 
substantial autocorrelation in returns for any of the four indices. 
The occasional bar crossing the confidence band — notably around 
lags 7–9 for ESGU and GSPC — is likely attributable to random 
variation, as approximately 1–2 spurious crossings are expected at 
the 95% confidence level across 30 lags. These results are consistent 
with weak-form market efficiency.

```{r acf-squared, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap="ACF of squared log returns — significant bars confirm volatility clustering (ARCH effects)."}
library(xts)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$ESGU))^2, main = "ACF — ESGU Squared", lag.max = 30)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$GSPC))^2, main = "ACF — GSPC Squared", lag.max = 30)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$IWDA))^2, main = "ACF — IWDA Squared", lag.max = 30)
acf(na.omit(as.numeric(log_returns$SUWS))^2, main = "ACF — SUWS Squared", lag.max = 30)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
In contrast, the ACF plots for the squared log returns reveal a 
striking pattern — large, statistically significant bars extending 
across many lags for all four series. For the US pair (ESGU and GSPC), 
autocorrelation in squared returns remains significant beyond lag 30, 
while the global pair (IWDA and SUWS) shows a similar but slightly 
less persistent pattern. This confirms the presence of strong ARCH 
effects: large returns in one period are systematically followed by 
further large returns, regardless of direction. This finding directly 
motivates the GARCH(1,1) modelling approach in Section 5.4, which 
formally captures and quantifies this volatility clustering.

### 5.4 Volatility Modelling (GARCH)

### 5.4.1 Volatility Modelling (GARCH (1,1))

While rolling volatility provides a useful visual summary of how 
volatility changes over time, it does not formally model the statistical
properties of volatility. To do this we fit a GARCH(1,1) model to the log return
series of each index. The GARCH(1,1) model captures two well-documented features
of financial return data: volatility clustering (periods of high volatility tend
to be followed by further high volatility) and mean reversion (volatility
$eventually returns to its long-run average).

The GARCH(1,1) model is specified as follows:

$$\sigma^2_t = \omega + \alpha \epsilon^2_{t-1} + \beta \sigma^2_{t-1}$$

Where $\sigma^2_t$ is the conditional variance at time $t$, 
$\epsilon^2_{t-1}$ is the squared return shock from the previous period 
(the ARCH term), and $\sigma^2_{t-1}$ is the conditional variance from 
the previous period (the GARCH term). The parameter $\alpha$ captures 
how strongly volatility reacts to new shocks, and $\beta$ captures how 
persistent volatility is over time. A sum of $\alpha + \beta$ close to 1 
indicates high volatility persistence.

```{r garch-models, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(rugarch)
library(xts)

garch_spec <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model     = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "norm"
)

garch_esgu <- ugarchfit(spec = garch_spec, data = na.omit(log_returns$ESGU),
                        solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
garch_gspc <- ugarchfit(spec = garch_spec, data = na.omit(log_returns$GSPC),
                        solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
garch_iwda <- ugarchfit(spec = garch_spec, data = na.omit(log_returns$IWDA),
                        solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
garch_suws <- ugarchfit(spec = garch_spec, data = na.omit(log_returns$SUWS),
                        solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
```

```{r garch-summary-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(rugarch)

extract_coef <- function(fit, name) {
  cf  <- coef(fit)
  ic  <- infocriteria(fit)
  a   <- cf["alpha1"]
  b   <- cf["beta1"]
  df <- data.frame(
    Series        = name,
    `ω`           = round(cf["omega"],  6),
    `α (ARCH)`    = round(a,            4),
    `β (GARCH)`   = round(b,            4),
    `α + β`       = round(a + b,        4),
    AIC           = round(ic[1],        4),
    BIC           = round(ic[2],        4),
    check.names   = FALSE
  )
  rownames(df) <- NULL    # <-- add this line here
  df                      # this line was already there
}

coef_table <- rbind(
  extract_coef(garch_esgu, "ESGU"),
  extract_coef(garch_gspc, "GSPC (S&P 500)"),
  extract_coef(garch_iwda, "IWDA"),
  extract_coef(garch_suws, "SUWS")
)

kable(coef_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr",
      caption = "GARCH(1,1) Parameter Estimates") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(5, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = "α + β close to 1 indicates high volatility persistence. AIC/BIC are model fit criteria (lower is better).",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)
```

The GARCH(1,1) estimates reveal highly consistent volatility dynamics 
across all four series. Alpha coefficients range from 0.097 to 0.162, 
indicating that between 10% and 16% of each period's volatility is 
driven by the magnitude of the previous period's return shock. Beta 
coefficients are uniformly high, ranging from 0.804 to 0.871, 
reflecting strong volatility persistence across all series. The sum 
of alpha and beta — a measure of overall volatility persistence — 
falls between 0.963 and 0.969 for all four indices, close to but 
below unity, confirming that volatility is mean-reverting but does 
so slowly.

Notably, the GARCH parameters are remarkably similar between ESG and 
conventional pairs. For the US pair, ESGU (α = 0.157, β = 0.806) and 
GSPC (α = 0.157, β = 0.806) are virtually identical. For the global 
pair, IWDA (α = 0.162, β = 0.804) shows slightly higher shock 
sensitivity than SUWS (α = 0.097, β = 0.871), though both exhibit 
similarly high persistence. This suggests that ESG screening does not 
materially alter the volatility structure of equity returns, and that 
both ESG and conventional indices are subject to the same underlying 
volatility dynamics during the sample period.

```{r garch-vol-plot}
# Extract and plot conditional volatility for all series
vol_df <- data.frame(
  Date = index(log_returns),
  ESGU = as.numeric(sigma(garch_esgu)),
  GSPC = as.numeric(sigma(garch_gspc)),
  IWDA = as.numeric(sigma(garch_iwda)),
  SUWS = as.numeric(sigma(garch_suws))
)

vol_long <- melt(vol_df, id.vars = "Date",
                 variable.name = "Series",
                 value.name = "Volatility")

ggplot(vol_long, aes(x = Date, y = Volatility, colour = Series)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2022-01-01"),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2022-03-01"), y = 0.045,
           label = "Rate hiking begins", size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "GARCH(1,1) Conditional Volatility",
       x = "Date", y = "Conditional Standard Deviation") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility plot refines the picture provided 
by the rolling volatility analysis. Unlike rolling volatility which uses 
a fixed window, GARCH volatility is model-based and reacts dynamically 
to new information. The two clear volatility spikes correspond to the 
COVID-19 market shock in March 2020 and the onset of the rate hiking 
cycle in early 2022.

### 5.4.2 Volatility Modelling (GARCH-X): Including Interest Rate Changes 

To extend the baseline GARCH(1,1) analysis, we estimate a GARCH-X 
model which incorporates changes in the 10-year US Treasury yield as 
an exogenous variable in the variance equation. This allows us to test 
directly whether interest rate changes have a significant effect on 
the conditional volatility of each series, over and above the 
volatility clustering already captured by the standard GARCH terms.

The GARCH-X model is specified as:
$$\sigma^2_t = \omega + \alpha \epsilon^2_{t-1} + \beta \sigma^2_{t-1} + \gamma \Delta r_t$$

Where $\Delta r_t$ is the change in the 10-year Treasury yield at time 
$t$, and $\gamma$ captures the direct effect of interest rate changes 
on conditional volatility.

```{r garch-x-models, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(rugarch)
library(xts)

# Align rate_diff with log_returns
rate_aligned <- merge(log_returns, rate_diff)
rate_aligned <- na.omit(rate_aligned)

# Extract aligned series
esgu_r <- rate_aligned$ESGU
gspc_r <- rate_aligned$GSPC
iwda_r <- rate_aligned$IWDA
suws_r <- rate_aligned$SUWS
rate_x <- as.matrix(rate_aligned$Rate_10Y)

# GARCH-X specification with external regressor in variance equation
garchx_spec <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(
    model        = "sGARCH",
    garchOrder   = c(1, 1),
    external.regressors = rate_x
  ),
  mean.model     = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "norm"
)

garchx_esgu <- ugarchfit(spec = garchx_spec, data = esgu_r,
                          solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
garchx_gspc <- ugarchfit(spec = garchx_spec, data = gspc_r,
                          solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
garchx_iwda <- ugarchfit(spec = garchx_spec, data = iwda_r,
                          solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
garchx_suws <- ugarchfit(spec = garchx_spec, data = suws_r,
                          solver = "hybrid", solver.control = list(trace = 0))
```

```{r garch-x-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(rugarch)

extract_garchx <- function(fit, name) {
  cf <- coef(fit)
  ic <- infocriteria(fit)
  df <- data.frame(
    Series     = name,
    `α (ARCH)` = round(cf["alpha1"],    4),
    `β (GARCH)`= round(cf["beta1"],     4),
    `γ (Rate)` = round(cf["vxreg1"],    8),
    `α + β`    = round(cf["alpha1"] + cf["beta1"], 4),
    AIC        = round(ic[1],           4),
    BIC        = round(ic[2],           4),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  rownames(df) <- NULL
  df
}

garchx_table <- rbind(
  extract_garchx(garchx_esgu, "ESGU"),
  extract_garchx(garchx_gspc, "GSPC (S&P 500)"),
  extract_garchx(garchx_iwda, "IWDA"),
  extract_garchx(garchx_suws, "SUWS")
)

kable(garchx_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr",
      caption = "GARCH-X Parameter Estimates — Including Interest Rate Changes") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(4, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = "γ captures the direct effect of interest rate changes on conditional volatility. A positive γ indicates that rate increases raise volatility.",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)
```
```{r check-alignment, include=FALSE}
cat("Dimensions of rate_x:", dim(rate_x), "\n")
cat("First few values of rate_x:\n")
print(head(rate_x))
cat("Any NAs:", sum(is.na(rate_x)), "\n")
cat("Any zeros:", sum(rate_x == 0, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
```
The GARCH-X estimates reveal that the exogenous interest rate term γ 
is effectively zero for all four series, indicating that daily changes 
in the 10-year Treasury yield do not have a direct measurable effect 
on the conditional volatility of these indices. This finding suggests 
that interest rate changes operate through return levels and relative 
performance rather than through volatility — a conclusion consistent 
with the VAR results in Section 5.5, which showed that rate changes 
Granger-cause the ESG-conventional spread in the global pair but not 
the US pair.

Comparing the GARCH-X model to the baseline GARCH(1,1), the α and β 
estimates are virtually unchanged across all series, and the AIC and 
BIC values are marginally higher in the GARCH-X model — suggesting 
that adding the interest rate variable does not improve model fit. 
Together, these results indicate that the standard GARCH(1,1) 
specification is sufficient to capture the volatility dynamics of 
these series, and that the role of interest rates is better captured 
through the return spread and regime analyses.

### 5.5 Vector Autoregression (VAR) Model

We use a VAR model in this project to ask, do past changes in interest rates help predict future changes in the ESG-conventional performance gap? Or in other words, does adding rate history improve our ability to predict the spread?

```{r var-model, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(vars)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# US pair VAR
spread_us  <- log_returns$ESGU - log_returns$GSPC
rate_d     <- rate_diff
var_us     <- merge(spread_us, rate_d)
var_us     <- na.omit(var_us)
colnames(var_us) <- c("Spread_US", "Rate_Change")
lag_us     <- VARselect(var_us, lag.max = 10, type = "const")$selection["AIC(n)"]
model_us   <- VAR(var_us, p = lag_us, type = "const")
granger_us <- causality(model_us, cause = "Rate_Change")

# Global pair VAR
spread_global  <- log_returns$IWDA - log_returns$SUWS
var_global     <- merge(spread_global, rate_d)
var_global     <- na.omit(var_global)
colnames(var_global) <- c("Spread_Global", "Rate_Change")
lag_global     <- VARselect(var_global, lag.max = 10, type = "const")$selection["AIC(n)"]
model_global   <- VAR(var_global, p = lag_global, type = "const")
granger_global <- causality(model_global, cause = "Rate_Change")

# Summary table
granger_table <- data.frame(
  Test          = c("Rate → US Spread", "Rate → Global Spread"),
  `F-statistic` = c(round(granger_us$Granger$statistic,     4),
                     round(granger_global$Granger$statistic, 4)),
  `p-value`     = c(round(granger_us$Granger$p.value,     4),
                     round(granger_global$Granger$p.value, 4)),
  Result        = c(ifelse(granger_us$Granger$p.value     < 0.05,
                           "Granger-causes", "Does not Granger-cause"),
                    ifelse(granger_global$Granger$p.value < 0.05,
                           "Granger-causes", "Does not Granger-cause")),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(granger_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrr",
      caption = "Granger Causality Tests — Interest Rate Changes and ESG Spreads") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(4, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = "H0: Rate_Change does not Granger-cause the ESG-conventional spread. Rejection at p < 0.05 indicates predictive power.",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)
```
The Granger causality results reveal an asymmetry between the two 
market pairs. For the US pair, changes in the 10-year Treasury yield 
do not significantly Granger-cause the ESGU-GSPC return spread 
(F = 1.13, p = 0.32), suggesting that the two US indices track each 
other too closely for rate movements to produce a meaningful 
differential. For the global pair, however, rate changes significantly 

Granger-cause the IWDA-SUWS spread (F = 23.39, p < 0.001), indicating 
that the interest rate environment has predictive power over the 
relative performance of ESG and conventional global indices. This 
finding is consistent with the structural differences between IWDA 
and SUWS in terms of sector composition and geographic exposure.

### 5.6 Regime Analysis: Pre- and Post-2022 Comparison

To examine whether the relationship between ESG and conventional indices 
changed with the interest rate environment, we split the sample into two 
subperiods: a pre-hiking period (January 2020 to December 2021) and a 
post-hiking period (January 2022 to December 2024). We compare mean 
returns, volatility, and the ESG-conventional spread across both regimes.
It simply cuts the data in half at January 2022 and compares the basic statistics on either side. Essentially, we are asking, did things change after the Fed started raising rates? 

```{r regime-analysis, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(xts)

pre  <- log_returns[index(log_returns) < as.Date("2022-01-01")]
post <- log_returns[index(log_returns) >= as.Date("2022-01-01")]

# Per series stats
series_stats <- function(data, period) {
  data.frame(
    Period     = period,
    Series     = c("ESGU", "GSPC", "IWDA", "SUWS"),
    Mean       = round(c(mean(data$ESGU), mean(data$GSPC),
                         mean(data$IWDA), mean(data$SUWS)), 5),
    Volatility = round(c(sd(data$ESGU), sd(data$GSPC),
                         sd(data$IWDA), sd(data$SUWS)), 5)
  )
}

# Spread stats separately
spread_table <- data.frame(
  Period        = c("Pre-2022", "Post-2022"),
  `Spread_US (bps)`     = c(round(mean(pre$ESGU  - pre$GSPC)  * 10000, 2),
                             round(mean(post$ESGU - post$GSPC) * 10000, 2)),
  `Spread_Global (bps)` = c(round(mean(pre$IWDA  - pre$SUWS)  * 10000, 2),
                             round(mean(post$IWDA - post$SUWS) * 10000, 2)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Main table
main_table <- rbind(
  series_stats(pre,  "Pre-2022"),
  series_stats(post, "Post-2022")
)

kable(main_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrr",
      caption = "Regime Analysis — Mean Returns and Volatility by Period") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(2, bold = TRUE) |>
  row_spec(4, extra_latex_after = "\\midrule") |>
  footnote(general = "Pre-2022: Jan 2020 to Dec 2021. Post-2022: Jan 2022 to Dec 2024.",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)

# Spread table
kable(spread_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrr",
      caption = "Regime Analysis — ESG vs Conventional Return Spread by Period") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 10) |>
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(general = "Spread = ESG index return minus conventional index return. Positive value indicates ESG outperformance.",
           general_title = "Note: ", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)
```

**Returns (H1)**
Mean daily returns declined across all four series in the post-2022 
period, consistent with the broader equity market headwinds associated 
with rising interest rates. ESGU fell from 0.083% to 0.029% per day, 
while GSPC fell from 0.073% to 0.027%. The global pair showed a similar 
pattern, with SUWS experiencing the sharpest decline — from 0.079% to 
just 0.011% per day. This provides partial support for H1: ESG indices 
did exhibit different return behaviour in the post-2022 period, 
particularly in the global pair where SUWS underperformed more 
substantially than its conventional counterpart IWDA.

**Volatility (H2)**
Volatility declined in the post-2022 period for all series, which may 
appear counterintuitive given the macroeconomic uncertainty of the 
rate-hiking cycle. However, this is largely explained by the inclusion 
of the COVID-19 market shock in the pre-2022 subsample — the extreme 
volatility clustering of March 2020 substantially inflates the pre-2022 
standard deviations. When comparing the two periods with this in mind, 
the results do not provide strong evidence that ESG indices exhibit 
materially different volatility dynamics from conventional indices, 
offering only limited support for H2. Both ESG and conventional series 
show similar volatility levels within each regime.

**ESG-Conventional Spread (H3)**
The spread analysis provides the most directly relevant evidence for 
H3. In the US pair, the spread between ESGU and GSPC was already 
negligible in the pre-2022 period (1.0 basis point) and remained so 
post-2022 (0.13 basis points), confirming that the two US indices 
track each other extremely closely regardless of the interest rate 
environment. 

For the global pair, however, a more meaningful pattern emerges. The 
IWDA-SUWS spread shifted from -1.51 basis points pre-2022 — indicating 
modest ESG outperformance — to +2.38 basis points post-2022, indicating 
conventional outperformance. This sign reversal is consistent with H3: 
the relationship between ESG and conventional indices did change across 
regimes, with the global ESG index underperforming its conventional 
counterpart during the rate-hiking period. This finding aligns with the 
theoretical argument of Pastor, Stambaugh and Taylor (2022) that the 
structural tilt of ESG indices toward growth stocks may disadvantage 
them in rising rate environments.

Overall, the regime analysis provides mixed but informative evidence. 
The US pair shows no meaningful ESG-conventional divergence in either 
period, suggesting that for large-cap US equities, ESG screening does 
not materially alter return or volatility dynamics. The global pair 
tells a more nuanced story, with a detectable shift in relative 
performance that is broadly consistent with the interest rate 
hypothesis tested in this paper.
